title: The Yadavas Rout Jarasandha's Army and Spare Him
story:
The two brothers rode out to meet an ocean. Jarasandha, seeing them come, cupped his hands to his mouth and shouted abuse across the field — insults for Krishna, and for Balarama a challenge: if you have any courage, come and fight; summon your fortitude and show it.

Behind the brothers, on the towers and terraces of Mathura, the women of the city had gathered to watch, and more than one swooned where she stood, overcome with grief and fear at the sight of that enormous host.

Krishna's chariot drove into the thick of it, and there he fought as he alone could. Like a wheel of fire that burns in an unbroken circle, his arrows streamed out — nock, draw, loose — without pause and without gap. Elephants with split foreheads crashed down among their own ranks. Horses fell with their necks severed. Chariots splintered like dry branches under a storm. Jarasandha's army was an ocean, dark and without a shore, and men said afterward that no one could have crossed it; but the one who waded into it, though he chose to fight in mortal form, was not measured by mortal measure. In the sky above, out of sight of the armies, the gods and the celestial singers gathered from all quarters to watch, and the field shone under their gathered light like the night sky.

In the middle of it all Balarama sought out Jarasandha himself. The Magadha king had spent his chariot, his horses and his charioteer in the press, and stood alone on the field — and Balarama seized him the way a lion seizes a lion, by the shoulders, so that the king of Magadha hung helpless in his grip. His army lay in ruins around him; his allies were dead or fled. The Vrishni soldiers closed in, and ropes were brought, and Jarasandha, the enemy of the house, was bound where he stood.

Then Krishna stayed the binding. "The Magadha is not to be slain," he said. "He will gather forces again."

Balarama's hands went still. Krishna spoke to the captive with words whose meaning was pure and plain, and then let him go. Jarasandha, released by the two lords of the world, stood a long moment in the shame of it — a shame softened only by the knowledge that every hero on the field counted him worthy of such handling. Then he turned and walked off the field, and no one stopped him.

All around him his host was gone. Krishna, his own strength unbroken, had crossed that ocean as if it had been a pond. As the news ran ahead of him, the people of Mathura poured out through the gates to meet him, free of their fever, carried on a wave of joy. Conches and kettledrums sounded from the walls; the streets were sprinkled with water and hung with banners; women stood on the rooftops and showered the returning chariots with garlands, curds and unbroken rice. The sun set on a city that had braced itself to die at dawn and could not stop celebrating at dusk. And the weapons that had come down from the sky for the battle were seen no more, as if they had never been.

Seventeen times after that day Jarasandha came again to Mathura, each time with an army reckoned in akshauhinis, and seventeen times the Vrishnis, by Krishna's splendor, destroyed his host and sent him home. He returned to Magadha with his life, and that was all he carried back.

The city sang on into the night. The king who had sworn to leave no Yadava alive had been spared by the very men he had come to destroy — and spared, as he himself suspected, for a purpose none of them could yet see.
reflection: Krishna lets Jarasandha walk away at the height of victory, knowing the man will return seventeen times. His mercy is not softness but strategy: Jarasandha's death belongs to a design larger than this one day's battle, and the release is the first move of it.
tradition_note: The Harivamsha splits this episode differently: there the fighting runs twenty-seven days, and it is a voice from the sky — not Krishna — that stays Balarama's hand and declares that Jarasandha must not yet die. The Bhagavata Purana, followed here, has Krishna himself release the captive.
content_note: Battle scene: the rout of an army is described with restraint, but includes slaughter imagery.
next_story_tease: But even as Mathura celebrated, a new enemy — one protected by a boon no weapon could break — was already marching out of the north.
